name: Maya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Maya, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya, 27, single, and I share a flat with my friend Priya, who's a hairdresser. I left school without finishing because things at home were messy, and I've had loads of jobs since: cafés, a call centre for six months, then the warehouse. I've been there just under a year. I'm good with money, weirdly, so I've got about ten months of bills put away and a bit in an index fund, which is a cheap fund that follows the whole stock market.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a distribution centre for electronics, so phones, headphones, chargers, that sort of thing. Half the building is normal aisles where I walk with a trolley, and the other half is a pilot zone where little robots bring the shelves to you and you just pick from a screen. I'm honestly not fast yet, I mix up the small boxes. But I love the robot zone. I keep asking the engineers what the error codes mean, and I look them up on my phone with an AI chatbot on my break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that'd be a bit disappointing for me, actually. I like the robot side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say online that the bosses oversold it to get investors excited, and the workers carried on doing the real work. I'd say it in a jokey way. At work I'd tell the engineers, 'Guess you're stuck with me asking questions then.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think fine, my job's safe, my savings grow. But I'd also be a bit bored. I was kind of hoping the robot zone would turn into a real career path for people like me who never finished school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and keep putting money into savings and the fund. I'd still try to get onto the maintenance team, because the robot zone exists already, even in this picture. I'd keep using the chatbot to learn the fault codes on my break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, maybe. Like a film that never gets to the good bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned people like you who didn't finish school. What does that path look like if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as it always has, I think. You get faster, maybe team leader in five years if you're lucky. Or you do a forklift licence. It's fine, it's a living, but it's not much of a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me really. I'd worry more about the people on agency contracts, because they're the ones let go when it's quiet. I'm on a proper contract, so I'm all right.

say: I'd joke online that bosses **oversold AI** to excite investors.
I'd tease the **engineers** that they're stuck with my questions.
think: My **job's safe** and savings grow, but I'd feel a bit **bored**.
I hoped the **robot zone** would become a real **career path**.
do: Keep working shifts and adding to **savings** and the **index fund**.
Keep trying for the **maintenance team**, using a chatbot to learn **fault codes**.
feel: **Calm**, with a slight **flatness**, like a film that never gets good.
S0.quote: I was kind of hoping the robot zone would turn into a real career path for people like me who never finished school.
fieldNote: She sees robots as an **opportunity**, not a threat: unusual for a junior picker.
Strong **savings and a fund** give her room to experiment.
Her concern is for **agency workers**, a progressive streak even when she's safe.

steps.text: Keep adding to savings and the index fund each month
Study robot fault codes with a chatbot on breaks
Apply to shadow the robot maintenance team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now this is the one I think is actually happening. The office is already using AI to plan the stock, I'm pretty sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, but only if workers get the training, not just the managers. I'd post about that, and I'd push it at the union meeting, because the training always goes to people who already have qualifications. At work I'd tell people to get into the robot zone while it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Robots spreading slowly means they need people to fix them and run them, and I'm already hanging around the engineers. My picking job might shrink, but I'm trying to leave it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this month for a place on the maintenance training, and I'd pay for an online electronics course myself if they said no. I'd use AI every day to study for it. I'd also help colleagues figure out the new apps, because a lot of them are scared of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I know that's not how most people on my aisle feel, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your aisle would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman called Bernadette who's been there twelve years, and she hates the scanners. She's fast with her hands but the new screens freeze her up. I'd worry they'd see her as slow when she's the best picker we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for a course yourself. How much would you spend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 500 or 600, out of savings. That's less than a month's rent. If it gets me off the floor and into maintenance, it pays back in a year.

I'd tell colleagues to get into the **robot zone** while it's small.

feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, while knowing her aisle feels differently.
S1.quote: My picking job might shrink, but I'm trying to leave it anyway.
fieldNote: She is **already moving**, so disruption looks like a door opening.
She worries for **older colleagues** who are fast with hands but frozen by screens.

steps.text: Ask the manager this month for a maintenance training place
Pay for an online electronics course from savings if refused
Use AI daily to study electronics and robot faults
Raise worker training access at the next union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. 2028 for thinking, and 2031 for robots that can do everything with their hands. Okay. That changes my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper safety net, like a basic income, a regular payment from the government for everyone, and fast. I'd go on marches. And I'd post a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even my big idea gets eaten. If AI can think like an engineer by 2028, then the robots basically diagnose themselves, and by 2031 they can fix each other too. So maintenance buys me maybe three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go into maintenance straight away, because three years of better pay is three years. I'd save hard, maybe get to eighteen months of bills. I'd look at what can't be done by a machine even then, like care work or something with people. And I'd join any campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not falling apart, I've got money and I can learn fast. But I can't see where I'm landing, and that's new for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'that's new for me'. What's usually the thing that gets you through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being quick to jump. Every job I've had, I've seen the next thing early and moved. In the fast picture, there's nowhere to jump to that the AI isn't already standing on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would be weirdly fine, because nobody wants a robot doing their hair, at least not for a long time. I'd probably joke that I'll come and sweep her salon floor. Half joke.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** from the government, fast.
I'd go on **marches** and post about it, probably too much.
think: AI that thinks like an engineer means **maintenance** buys only **three years**.
By **2031** robots could even fix each other, so no safe career remains.
do: Move into **maintenance** straight away for three years of better pay.
Save hard to reach about **eighteen months** of bills.
Look into **people work** like care, and back basic income campaigns.
feel: **Anxious**, because she can't see where she's landing.
Still steadied by **money and learning** fast.
S2.quote: In the fast picture, there's nowhere to jump to that the AI isn't already standing on.
fieldNote: Her usual strategy, **jump early**, fails when everything moves at once.
She works through the **three-year robot gap** and sees even maintenance as short-term.
She is **anxious, not alarmed**, because savings and quick learning still give her some control.

steps.text: Move into robot maintenance straight away for higher pay
Save towards eighteen months of bills
Join a campaign for a government basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for thinking, robots by 2034. That's eight years for my hands. Okay, I can do something with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it right, if governments get going now. I'd push the union to get training funds before it arrives. Online I'd share stuff about free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think it's still big, but there's room to build something. Maintenance would last me five, maybe six years, which is enough to save a lot and work out the next thing. Maybe something with people in it, where being human is the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into maintenance within the year, and I'd save half of the extra pay. I'd do an evening course in something people-heavy too, maybe youth work, just to have a second door. And I'd keep investing in the fund, small amounts every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like moving house, lots to do, a bit stressful, but I can see the new place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Youth work is a big jump from robots. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because of where I come from. If someone had sat with me at fifteen, I might have finished school. A machine could teach maths, sure, but sitting with a kid who's having a bad week feels like it stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time make you less political?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, more, in a way. With five years there's actually time to win something, like retraining money or shorter weeks. In the fast one it feels like shouting at a train.

I'd push the union to win **training funds** before it arrives.
think: **Maintenance** would last five or six years, enough to save and plan.
I'd look for work where **being human** is the point.

Take an **evening course** in youth work as a second door.

S3.quote: Sitting with a kid who's having a bad week feels like it stays human.

steps.text: Move into robot maintenance within the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then 2039 for the hands-on robots. I'd be nearly 40. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: great, now let's use the decade properly, with free training and a fair share for workers. I'd be the annoying one at union meetings asking for a plan. At work I'd tell people this is the moment to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is my best case. I get a whole career in maintenance first, maybe even become a proper technician with a certificate. Then I'd move into something with people later in my thirties, with money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance training this year and get a recognised qualification within two or three years. I'd keep investing every month. I'd keep using AI tools daily to learn faster, and maybe teach a lunchtime session for colleagues on how to use the chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost excited. I'd worry about other people more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older pickers who've been there fifteen years. I think older pickers will have ten years' warning and probably still not move, because nobody ever helped them learn new stuff before. That's on the company as much as them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could knock you off course here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company decided to bring in its own technicians from outside instead of training people like me. That happens a lot. Then I'd just go to another warehouse, there are plenty round here.

I'd tell colleagues this is **the moment to learn**.
think: This is my **best case**: a whole career in **maintenance** first.
I'd move into **people work** later in my thirties, with money saved.

Keep **investing** a set amount every month.

fieldNote: A decade fits her plan perfectly: **maintenance career**, then people work.

steps.text: Start maintenance training this year and qualify within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'd be broke, I wouldn't, but because there'd be nowhere to jump. What would help is a basic income and free training that's open to people without exams, not just graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets picked for training. In my warehouse, training always goes to the people who already have certificates, so the people who need it most get it last. If they don't fix that, nothing else works.

headlineQuote: In my warehouse, training always goes to the people who already have certificates, so the people who need it most get it last.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old picker** at an electronics warehouse with a robot **pilot zone** she loves.
She left school early, has **ten months saved** plus an index fund, and uses AI chatbots daily.
She sees slow change as a **door into maintenance**, and only gets anxious when AGI comes fast.
Her backup plan is **youth work**, shaped by her own messy teenage years.
Her politics are about **fair access to training** for people without exams.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be nowhere to jump that AI hadn't reached.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and **free training** open to people without exams.
